claims.text: The identity of X in CrFeCoNiX controls whether a protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C.
Oxide protection is governed by a balance between thermodynamically favored selective oxidation and kinetic barriers from interfacial diffusion.
Al incorporation promotes nucleation of alumina, potentially together with chromia.
The oxides promoted by Al are slow-growing, coherent, and effective diffusion barriers.
Si incorporation promotes nucleation of slow-growing, coherent silica, potentially together with chromia.
Mn is the major oxide-forming element in CrMnFeCoNi and produces nonprotective oxides.
High Mn diffusivity and low oxide adhesion cause rapid growth of a poorly adherent, crack- and spall-prone manganese oxide scale.
Slower diffusion and high oxide stability in Al-containing alloys produce a thin, coherent, self-healing barrier.
Slower diffusion and high oxide stability in Si-containing alloys produce a thin, coherent, self-healing barrier.
The controlled comparison varies X among Al, Si, and Mn while using X-free CrFeCoNi as the baseline and holding processing history constant.
The hypothesis applies to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The proposed exposure is a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere above 900 °C for approximately 100 h or longer.
Oxide phase composition, scale thickness, and adhesion or coherence constitute the structural mediator between X selection and oxidation performance.
Relative to CrFeCoNi, the Al-containing alloy will form a thinner, more coherent and adherent scale with lower mass gain.
Relative to CrFeCoNi, the Si-containing alloy will form a thinner, more coherent and adherent scale with lower mass gain.
Relative to CrFeCoNi and the Al- and Si-containing alloys, the Mn-containing alloy will develop a thicker, less coherent scale with greater spallation and mass gain.
Grain size, phase distribution, and processing variations can alter oxidation resistance and the quantitative differences among the alloys.
Failure of the Al- and Si-containing samples to show consistently thinner, more coherent scales and lower mass gain than both the Mn-containing and baseline samples would falsify the hypothesis.
